query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In these iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy alloy nanoparticles, the onset of premelting is triggered by the preferential local melting (or surface segregation) of the lower-melting-point component (primarily copper), which forms liquid-like regions at the nanoparticle surfaces that promote accelerated diffusion and subsequent homogenization in the melt, a process further enabled by multicomponent mixing.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, single‐phase, equiatomic HEA nanoparticles with a uniform distribution of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating with a gradual temperature increase from below the solidus, through the premelting regime, and into full melting.
generation.conditions: Ambient pressure and inert atmosphere with precise temperature control; nanoparticle sizes where surface-to-volume effects are prominent.
generation.structural_mediator: Local elemental segregation and liquid–solid interfacial regions (especially copper-enriched areas) that form due to differences in individual melting points and interatomic interactions.
generation.mechanism: Because copper has a lower melting point compared to the other principal elements, it begins to form nano-liquid regions at the particle surface or interfaces before the bulk melting occurs; this local melting lowers the cohesive energy and enables accelerated diffusion that, with further heating, rapidly homogenizes the alloy, a process further enabled by multicomponent mixing.
generation.predicted_outcome: Premelting will manifest as early onset of surface morphology changes (e.g., local spreading or slight reshaping seen in imaging) at temperatures moderately below the expected melting point, followed by a rapid transition to a homogeneous liquid phase as temperature increases. The observation of a distinct Cu-enrichment at early liquid‐like regions is anticipated.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles undergoing conventional homogeneous melting without prior segregation; i.e., materials where no differential premelting behavior is observed.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HEA nanoparticles composed of Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu in near-equiatomic ratios and within sizes and heating rates where surface and finite-size effects are significant (typically in the nanoscale regime under moderate thermal gradients).
generation.uncertainty: Exact temperature offsets, the degree of copper enrichment, and the quantitative extent of local melting may vary with particle size, heating rate, and slight compositional deviations. It is also uncertain if other elements contribute significantly to premelting in some processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in-situ high-resolution imaging (e.g., neutron radiography or high-temperature TEM) of single HEA nanoparticles during a controlled heating ramp. Simultaneously conduct spatially resolved elemental mapping (using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy or similar techniques) to monitor any local compositional variations, particularly looking for Cu enrichment at the nanoparticle surfaces or interfaces as temperature approaches the premelting regime.
measurements: Nanoparticle shape and morphology changes as a function of temperature
Elemental distribution profiles (with emphasis on Cu) across nanoparticle cross-sections
Onset temperature of local liquid-like behavior compared to known melting points of individual components
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no evidence of selective copper segregation or early onset local melting (prior to the bulk melting point) is observed under these conditions, and the nanoparticle morphology and composition remain homogeneous until complete melting, then the hypothesis that differential premelting (driven by Cu) governs the melting behavior is falsified.

The CoCrCuNi alloy has been previously shown to solidify into a uniform dendritic microstructure from arc-melting [], which is indicative that the microstructure evolved from a single-phase liquid as opposed to the large-scale macroscopic-phase separation that has been observed in similar alloys of CoCrCu [] and CoCrCuFe []. However, there are no reported slow cooling solidification studies on the CoCrCuNi alloy. Previous neutron imaging of the CoCrCu by the present authors resulted in neutron radiographs of the CoCrCu displaying the buttons melting and separating based on density []. The stacking of the liquid immiscible phases of CoCr-rich liquid and Cu-rich liquid was characterized by their differences in neutron attenuation. The same experiment was essentially repeated for this work with the equiatomic addition of Ni buttons such that the equiatomic CoCrCu becomes equiatomic CoCrCuNi once melting and dissolution has occurred. This allows for a more equilibrium solidification due to the slow cooling, as well as an opportunity to image the remixing of the immiscible CoCr-rich and Cu-rich liquid phases.
